title: Kernel Performance Tuning
blurb: Tests arithmetic intensity and the roofline, the ridge point and how to classify a kernel, occupancy and the per-SM block and thread caps, theoretical against achieved occupancy, register spills, and instruction-level parallelism as a separate lever.

ideas.title: The ridge point and classifying a kernel

refLinks.label: §43.2.2 Occupancy: Why Launch Configuration Alone Changes Performance
§43.2.3 Instruction-Level Parallelism: A Third, Independent Lever

questions.prompt: What is a kernel's arithmetic intensity?
options: FLOPs per second, as a share of the GPU's peak
Bytes moved per second, measured in GB/s
Floating-point operations per byte of memory moved
Threads launched per SM, as a share of the maximum
questions.explanation: Intensity is FLOPs divided by bytes, in FLOPs/byte. Low intensity means memory-bound, high means compute-bound. GB/s and GFLOP/s are achieved rates, and threads per SM is occupancy.

questions.prompt: The roofline kernel reads one fp32 value, does REPEAT fused multiply-adds (2 FLOPs each) and writes one fp32 value. What is its intensity at REPEAT = 16, in FLOPs/byte?
questions.explanation: FLOPs = 16 × 2 = 32. Bytes = 4 read + 4 written = 8. 32 / 8 = 4 FLOPs/byte, matching the table.

questions.prompt: On the roofline plot, what does the sloped part of the line represent?
options: The memory-bandwidth ceiling, which binds at low intensity
Latency, which grows as kernels get longer
Occupancy, rising as more warps become resident
The compute ceiling, which binds at low intensity before memory does
questions.explanation: At low intensity, performance rises with intensity because bandwidth is the limit. The flat line is the compute ceiling at high intensity. They meet at the knee.

questions.prompt: From REPEAT = 1 to 64 in the sweep, GB/s stayed near peak while GFLOP/s climbed. Why?
options: The L2 cache grew to hold the extra FMAs.
Occupancy rose with REPEAT, hiding more latency.
The kernel was compute-bound, so memory traffic didn't matter at all.
The kernel was memory-bound, so the extra arithmetic was nearly free.
questions.explanation: Below the knee the GPU waits on memory either way, so more FMAs per element ride along on the same traffic. Past REPEAT = 256, GFLOP/s plateaus and GB/s falls.

questions.prompt: The reference rig peaks at about 118,600 GFLOP/s and 1,986 GB/s. What is its ridge point in FLOPs/byte? Give a whole number.
questions.explanation: ridge = peak FLOPs / peak bandwidth = 118,600 / 1,986 = 59.7, about 60 FLOPs/byte.

questions.prompt: Using classify_kernel with a ridge of about 60, how is an elementwise add, c = a + b in fp32, classified?
options: Compute-bound, since every element needs an add
Compute-bound, since its intensity is exactly at the ridge
Memory-bound, at 1 FLOP per 12 bytes, far below the ridge
It can't be classified without knowing the block size
questions.explanation: One add per element, with 12 bytes moved (two reads, one write), gives about 0.08 FLOPs/byte. That is far below 60, so bandwidth is the limit. Block size doesn't enter the formula.

questions.prompt: Why does Procedure 43.1 say to classify a kernel before choosing an optimisation?
options: nvcc needs the classification to choose an instruction set.
The right fix depends on which ceiling binds.
Classification sets the block size, which must be fixed before tuning.
Only memory-bound kernels can be profiled with ncu.
questions.explanation: A memory-bound kernel wants fewer bytes or more reuse. A compute-bound one wants fewer or cheaper operations. Optimising the wrong side yields nothing.

questions.prompt: Chapter 47 fuses several elementwise operations into one kernel. Where does that move them on the roofline, and why does it help?
options: Rightward: several operations share one memory round trip.
Upward past the compute ceiling, since fused kernels use Tensor Cores.
Leftward. Fusing adds memory traffic, which the GPU handles better.
Nowhere. Fusion only reduces kernel launch count.
questions.explanation: Each separate elementwise kernel reads and writes memory. Fused, the data moves once and several operations run on it, so intensity rises while the kernel was memory-bound. Fusion can't exceed the compute ceiling.

questions.prompt: What is occupancy?
options: Resident warps on an SM, as a share of the most it could hold
The share of shared memory that a block allocates
The share of time the GPU spends computing rather than copying
The share of SMs that a kernel launch uses at all
questions.explanation: Low occupancy means fewer warps to switch to when one stalls, so the SM idles more. It is the latency-hiding argument from Chapter 38, made measurable.

refLinks.label: §43.2.2 Occupancy: Why Launch Configuration Alone Changes Performance

questions.prompt: The rig allows 1,536 threads per SM. With 1,024-thread blocks, how many threads of that capacity sit unused?
questions.explanation: Only one 1,024-thread block fits (1536 // 1024 = 1), leaving 1536 − 1024 = 512 threads idle. That is why block 1024 slowed to 0.1209 ms.

questions.prompt: With 32-thread blocks, the SM's cap of 24 resident blocks binds first. Of the 48 warps an SM can hold, what percentage is used?
questions.explanation: 24 blocks × 1 warp each = 24 warps, and 24 / 48 = 50%, which matches the theoretical figure for block 32.

questions.prompt: Why was block size 128 the fastest in the sweep?
options: 128 threads fit exactly in one warp, so there is no divergence.
1,536 / 128 = 12 blocks fit, filling all 48 warps without hitting either cap.
128 is the largest size that avoids register spills on this particular kernel.
Smaller blocks always run faster, and 128 was the smallest tested.
questions.explanation: Small blocks hit the 24-block cap before filling warps. Huge blocks waste thread capacity. 128 sits in the band that satisfies both. A warp is 32 threads, and 32 was the smallest size tested.

refLinks.label: §43.2.2 Occupancy: Why Launch Configuration Alone Changes Performance

questions.prompt: Higher occupancy always means a faster kernel. What does Procedure 43.2 say?
options: Yes, as long as the kernel is compute-bound.
No. Higher occupancy always slows a kernel down.
No. It's needed, not sufficient. Measure the time.
Yes. Occupancy is the single number that sets kernel speed.
questions.explanation: A compute-bound kernel already saturating the ALUs gains nothing from more warps. The worked example backs this: block 512 had the highest achieved occupancy, but block 128 was fastest.

questions.prompt: How does cudaOccupancyMaxActiveBlocksPerMultiprocessor differ from ncu's achieved occupancy?
options: They are the same number, reported by two tools.
The first predicts from resources. ncu measures the real run.
The first counts threads, and ncu counts blocks.
The first measures the run, while ncu only predicts from the launch configuration.
questions.explanation: The CUDA query is a resource-based prediction. ncu reports achieved occupancy from real execution, which was lower at every block size in the worked example.

questions.prompt: Block 64 predicted 100% occupancy but achieved 44%. Block 1024 predicted 66.67% and achieved 61.8%. Which ran faster, and what does that show?
options: Block 1024, slightly. Achieved occupancy predicted better.
Block 64, by far, as its 100% theoretical figure predicts.
Block 64, because smaller blocks always beat larger ones.
They tied exactly, since occupancy doesn't affect speed.
questions.explanation: Block 1024 took 0.1209 ms and block 64 took 0.1218 ms. Ranking by theoretical occupancy would get this backwards. Achieved occupancy did better, though still not perfectly.

questions.prompt: What does instruction-level parallelism give a thread?
options: More warps on its SM to switch to when it stalls
Independent instructions in flight while one result is pending
A second SM to run on when its own SM is busy
A wider memory transaction for each load it makes
questions.explanation: ILP is about one thread's own instruction stream. Having other warps to switch to is occupancy, a separate lever. The chapter shows both matter independently.

refLinks.label: §43.2.3 Instruction-Level Parallelism: A Third, Independent Lever

questions.prompt: Why is fmaSingleChain slower than fmaFourChains?
options: The four-chain kernel uses Tensor Cores and the other doesn't.
The single chain runs at lower occupancy, with fewer warps per SM.
Each FMA waits for the last one's result. Four chains let FMAs overlap.
The single chain does four times as many FMAs as the four-chain kernel.
questions.explanation: Both do 200 FMAs per thread at block size 128 and the same occupancy. The only difference is whether the hardware has independent work to overlap. Registers were 8 against 10, both far from any limit.

refLinks.label: §43.2.3 Instruction-Level Parallelism: A Third, Independent Lever

questions.prompt: The single chain took 0.0873 ms and four chains 0.0723 ms. What is the speedup? Give two decimal places.
questions.explanation: 0.0873 / 0.0723 = 1.21, from restructuring the same arithmetic at identical occupancy.

questions.prompt: What is the risk in adding many more accumulators to raise ILP further?
options: The compiler will merge them back into one chain, undoing the change entirely
Each accumulator adds a memory transaction per iteration
The output becomes less accurate with every accumulator added
More live registers per thread, which can cut occupancy or cause spills
questions.explanation: Procedure 43.4 warns that more independent state means more registers, and past some point that trades one bottleneck for another. Check usage with --ptxas-options=-v.

questions.prompt: ptxas reports spill stores and spill loads for a kernel. What does that mean?
options: It ran out of registers and uses slow local memory.
The kernel was compiled for the wrong compute capability.
Shared memory overflowed into the L2 cache.
The kernel has a correctness bug that corrupts some results.
questions.explanation: Spilling is correctness-neutral but costs performance. The common mistake is ignoring it because the build succeeded.

questions.prompt: What does -maxrregcount=32 do, and what is the trade-off?
options: Caps registers per thread to raise occupancy, at the risk of spilling
Caps threads per block at 32, so each block is one warp
Limits the kernel to 32 SMs, leaving the rest for other work
Reserves 32 registers for the driver, so that kernels launch faster
questions.explanation: Fewer registers per thread lets more threads fit, but if the kernel needs more, the compiler spills to slow local memory.

bookExercises.prompt: Define "arithmetic intensity" in your own words, and state which regime (memory-bound or compute-bound) a kernel with very low arithmetic intensity falls into.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Arithmetic intensity is the number of floating-point operations performed per byte of memory moved (FLOPs/byte). A kernel with very low arithmetic intensity falls in the memory-bound regime. Its runtime is set by how fast data can be moved, not by how fast the arithmetic can be computed.

bookExercises.prompt: Define "occupancy," and name the CUDA runtime function this chapter uses to measure it for a specific kernel rather than guessing.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Occupancy is the ratio of actually-resident warps on a streaming multiprocessor to the hardware maximum it could support. This chapter measures it with `cudaOccupancyMaxActiveBlocksPerMultiprocessor`, rather than guessing from block size alone.

bookExercises.prompt: Using Listing 43.1 and this chapter's reference-rig peak numbers (~118,600 GFLOP/s, ~1,986 GB/s), classify a kernel that moves 4 bytes per element and performs 8 FLOPs per element as memory-bound or compute-bound, showing the intensity and ridge-point values used.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Intensity $I = 8 \text{ FLOPs} / 4 \text{ bytes} = 2$ FLOPs/byte. Ridge point $R = 118{,}600 / 1{,}986 \approx 60$ FLOPs/byte. Since $I = 2 < R = 60$, the kernel is memory-bound.

bookExercises.prompt: Using the roofline sweep table, explain in one or two sentences why GB/s falls steadily from `REPEAT=256` onward even though the kernel still reads and writes exactly the same two memory locations per element as at `REPEAT=1`.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: As `REPEAT` grows, total time grows (more FMAs per element), but the bytes moved per element stay fixed at 8 (one 4-byte read, one 4-byte write). GB/s is bytes-moved divided by time, so as time grows with no corresponding growth in bytes moved, the GB/s figure necessarily falls. The kernel is doing more compute per byte, not moving more bytes faster.

bookExercises.prompt: Using the occupancy sweep table and this chapter's reported `max_threads_per_multi_processor = 1536`, compute how many blocks per SM fit at block size 256, and state whether that matches the "max active blk/SM" column's measured value of 6.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: $1{,}536 / 256 = 6$ blocks per SM by the thread-count cap alone. This matches the measured value of 6 max active blocks/SM at block size 256, confirming thread count (not the 24-block architectural cap, which would allow more) is the binding constraint at this block size.

bookExercises.prompt: A colleague proposes always launching kernels with block size 1024 "to maximise threads per block." Using this chapter's measured occupancy sweep, write the two or three sentences you'd say back.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Larger blocks don't automatically mean more parallelism. The occupancy sweep shows block size 1,024 fits only 1 block/SM (32 resident warps), *fewer* than block size 512's 48 resident warps, because the 1,536-thread-per-SM ceiling caps how many blocks of a given size can be co-resident. "Maximise threads per block" ignores this ceiling. The actual goal is maximising resident warps, which the sweep shows peaks around block size 256-512, not 1,024.

bookExercises.prompt: A kernel is confirmed compute-bound by Procedure 43.1. Propose one optimisation from this chapter's Trade-offs section that would plausibly help, and one from Chapter 40 that would not, explaining why in each case.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Reducing redundant arithmetic (this chapter's compute-bound remedy) would plausibly help, since it directly reduces the FLOPs the compute-bound kernel must perform. Improving memory coalescing (Chapter 40's remedy) would not help a confirmed compute-bound kernel, since by definition its runtime is set by FLOPs throughput, not memory bandwidth. Chapter 40's fixes only pay off in the memory-bound regime.

bookExercises.prompt: Read the original Williams, Waterman, and Patterson roofline paper's introduction. Summarise, in a few sentences, how the paper's "ridge point" concept compares to this chapter's measured knee between `REPEAT=64` and `REPEAT=256`, and whether the paper's framing anticipated GPU-specific caps like resident-blocks-per-SM.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Discussion only. The roofline paper's ridge point is architecture-general (peak FLOPs / peak bandwidth), matching this chapter's own ridge-point calculation closely. Whether the original paper anticipated GPU-specific caps like resident-blocks-per-SM is a fair question to investigate. The paper's core roofline concept predates modern GPU occupancy constraints becoming a widely-discussed secondary bottleneck, so the occupancy sweep in this chapter likely extends beyond what the original framing directly covers.

bookExercises.prompt: Using this chapter's achieved-vs-theoretical occupancy table, identify the one block size where theoretical occupancy *understates* how fast the kernel actually runs relative to another block size with higher theoretical occupancy, and state which of the two occupancy numbers correctly predicts the measured wall-clock ordering.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Block 1024 (theoretical 66.67%) is measured slightly faster (0.1209 ms) than block 64 (theoretical 100%, 0.1218 ms), the opposite of what theoretical occupancy alone predicts. Achieved occupancy correctly predicts this ordering: block 1024's achieved occupancy (61.80%) is higher than block 64's (44.00%), matching which one actually ran faster. Theoretical occupancy is a resource-based prediction from launch configuration alone; achieved occupancy, measured from the kernel's real execution via `ncu --section Occupancy`, is the number that tracks wall-clock time here.
